song.title: One In A Million!
song.author: Mark, Helen and Naomi Johnson
song.summary: A strong and catchy song for Mother’s Day, with thought-provoking lyrics reminding us that nobody is perfect, but that even on our grumpy days, ‘she’s the best one for me’.
song.teachingTips:
• The melody in the second half of the chorus has some semitone intervals. Some children may find it difficult to hear these initially so take time to repeat the melody slowly so that each note is clear and sung exactly at the right pitch.
  • Encourage raised eyebrows and smiles on the ‘Sometimes’ notes in the verses to make sure the children leap up to this note, as it’s an easy one to sing flat if you’re not careful.
  • As an exercise in learning about phrasing and call-and-response singing, divide the group in two and have both groups sing one short phrase to the other throughout the verses, joining together for a rousing chorus!

  • To recognize use of call-and-response repeated melodies in music
  • To compose call-and-response melodies and play these on instruments, using lyrics on a given theme
","title":"What’s achievable","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/green-star-1614702483w2iKm.png"}},{"key":"6b9a8b9677189e5c","layout":"icon-bullet","attributes":{"body":"

Amplified sound system; Internet; tuned percussion instruments; black/white board

","title":"What you need","noMargin":false,"image":"https://assets.sparkyard.com/uploads/icons/blue-wrench-16147025258WedI.png"}},{"key":"bdf45fdcd3c2db36","layout":"wysiwyg","attributes":{"body":"

Using just two notes, sing some questions and answers. Starting with the notes F and A, sing a question such as What’s your favourite food? Try to arrange the notes as you sing so that you end on the higher note (A), giving the feel of a question. Then, answer (e.g. I like hamburgers) ending on the lower note (F).

Next, working in pairs, distribute tuned percussion instruments or keyboards and write a selection of notes on the board to use to compose simple melodies e.g. C E G or D F A. Ask the children to create melodic patterns as a musical call and response, one asking questions and the other answering. Suggest a theme for their musical conversation and encourage them to write lyrics for topics such as ‘Things they talk about with Mum’ or ‘Great things Mum does for me’. Melodies should be simple and use just a few notes that repeat or echo, like the call-and-response examples in One In A Million! or Chuck Berry’s School Day.

Children should write their melodies down using the names of the notes and some form of notation to help them recall their tunes for the next lesson or even sing for their mums on Mother’s Day!
